`tests/Trireme.test.ts` used `<Unit>transport`. Node 24 strips types itself when `ts-mocha` does not intercept the file, and its stripper rejects the angle-bracket form outright:
SyntaxError: The angle-bracket syntax for type assertions, `<T>expr`, is not supported in type strip mode.

So the whole suite aborted before running a single test. With `expr as T` all 206 pass. The two forms mean the same thing; angle brackets are also ambiguous with JSX, which is why TypeScript discourages them.

Stage 2 of the engine serialisation plan. Nineteen packages call `Math.random()`, so nothing about a game is reproducible: no replay testing, and a save/load cycle would change the next combat result.

Overriding `Math.random` globally at worker boot would fix that for one game and needs no engine change at all — but it cannot survive Stage 3, where two `Game`s in one process would share the override and interleave their draws. So the generator is injected instead, with this module's `instance` as the default everywhere, which is the pattern `core-spaceship` already used.

`calls()` is the part that is easy to leave out and expensive to add later. A save recording only the seed would restart the stream rather than resume it, so a game saved before a battle and reloaded would fight it differently. mulberry32 makes `restore(seed, calls)` O(1) rather than a replay, because its state after n draws is `seed + n * increment` (mod 2^32).

It is deliberately its own package rather than part of `core-rule`: four of the nineteen consumers do not depend on `core-rule`, and making them pull in the rule engine to get a random number would be the wrong trade.

`attempt()` breaks priority ties with a random draw so that alternative strategies get tried, and had no parameter to redirect, so the constructor gains one defaulting to `core-random`'s shared instance.

This does not make `tests/StrategyRegistry.test.ts` deterministic. That test asserts a particular call order while the tie it depends on is broken randomly, and the default instance is seeded from the clock, so it still fails roughly three runs in eight. Passing it a fixed generator makes it consistent but not correct: it passes for seeds 1-5 and 11 and fails for 7, so a fixed seed would only freeze a lucky one. The test needs its own fix — most likely giving the strategies distinct priorities so the tiebreak never decides the outcome — which is not this stage's to make.

A rest parameter cannot be followed by another and inserting one ahead of it would break every existing call, which has to keep working for this to stay a range-compatible `0.1.x` release. `core-diplomacy`'s `Interaction` already uses this pattern.
